lesson.title: Levels of Ecological Organization: From One Organism to the Whole Biosphere
lesson.summary: Ecologists study life at a series of nested levels, organism, population, community, ecosystem, and biosphere, with each level built from the units of the level below it and revealing questions that do not exist at smaller scales.
lesson.body:
Ecology is the study of how organisms interact with each other and with their physical environment. Because those interactions happen at very different scales, from a single animal's behavior to patterns spanning the entire planet, ecologists organize their questions into a series of nested levels, each one built out of the units of the level below it.

The organism level is the starting point: a single individual living thing. At this level, ecologists (often working closely with physiologists) ask how an individual meets its basic needs, such as acquiring energy, avoiding predators, tolerating its physical environment, and reproducing.

The population level groups together all the individuals of the same species living in the same area at the same time, capable of interbreeding with one another. This is the level where questions about population size, density, and growth become meaningful, questions that later chapters in this unit build out in detail.

The community level expands further to include all the different species populations living and interacting in the same area, whether those interactions are competition for resources, predator-prey relationships, or various forms of symbiosis. A community is not just a list of species present in a place, but the network of interactions among them.

The ecosystem level adds the physical, nonliving environment on top of the community: all the organisms in an area together with the physical surroundings they interact with, such as soil, water, and climate. At the ecosystem level, questions shift toward how energy flows through a system, such as from sunlight to plants to the animals that eat them, and how nutrients cycle between living organisms and the nonliving environment.

Finally, the biosphere is the sum of every ecosystem on Earth, the global zone spanning the atmosphere, land, and water where life exists at all. It represents ecology at its widest possible scale.

Put together, the hierarchy runs organism, then population, then community, then ecosystem, then biosphere, with each level nested inside and built from the level before it: populations are made of organisms, communities are made of populations, ecosystems are communities plus their physical surroundings, and the biosphere is the sum of all ecosystems. Ecologists choose whichever level matches the question they are asking, and keeping this hierarchy straight makes it much easier to follow more specific topics, such as the study of populations, which the next several chapters focus on in detail.
